title: A loss function is a landscape
summary: A model's parameters are dials and its loss measures how badly it fits. Plotting the loss against one parameter gives a curve; against two it gives a surface over a map of settings, usually drawn as a contour map. Training is a search for low ground on that landscape, which for real networks has billions of dimensions.
llm_link: For a language model, every point of the landscape is one full setting of its billions of weights, and the height there is the average cross-entropy on the training text (lesson 3.7).
key_ideas: Each setting of the parameters is a point; the loss at that point is its height.
One parameter: a curve, loss against w. Two parameters: a surface over the (w, b) plane.
Contour lines join settings with equal loss; close together means steep, far apart means flat.
Mean squared error of a line y = w·x + b: average of (yᵢ − (w·xᵢ + b))² over the data.

quiz.q: On a contour map of a loss, contour lines are packed closely together in one region. What does that tell you?
options: The loss changes quickly there: the ground is steep
The model has fewer parameters there
quiz.explain: Each line is a fixed step in loss. Many lines in a short distance means the loss changes fast, like a steep hillside on a hiking map.

quiz.q: Predict the result: data (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6) and the model y = w·x. What is the mean squared error at w = 1?
quiz.explain: The errors are 2 − 1 = 1, 4 − 2 = 2 and 6 − 3 = 3; the squares are 1, 4 and 9; their mean is 14 / 3.

quiz.q: In the same example, where is the bottom of the loss curve?
quiz.explain: y = 2x passes through every point, so every error is 0 and the loss is at its minimum, 0.

quiz.q: What is a single point on the (w, b) map?
options: One complete model: a specific line
quiz.explain: Choosing w and b fixes the whole line. The landscape's height at that point is how badly that particular line fits the data.

quiz.q: For a large language model, what are the coordinates of its loss landscape?
options: All of its weights, billions of numbers
Just two numbers, w and b
quiz.explain: Every weight is one dial, so the landscape lives in a space with as many dimensions as the model has parameters. Its height is the training cross-entropy.

problems.title: The height of the landscape
problems.prompt:
Write mse(w, b, xs, ys): the mean squared error of the line y = w*x + b on the data. For each point the error is y − (w*x + b); square it, then average over all points.

mse(1.0, 0.0, xs, ys)   # 5.036
mse(1.29, 1.33, xs, ys) # 0.0278 (the best fit)

tests.code:

tests.code:

b = mse(0.0, 0.0, [1, 1], [2, 2])

problems.title: Walk along the curve
problems.prompt:
With b fixed at 0, the loss is a curve in w. Write lowest_w(ws, xs, ys) that evaluates the loss for every candidate in the list ws and returns the candidate with the smallest loss. (mse is provided.)

ws = [0.5 + 0.01 * k for k in range(200)]   # 0.50, 0.51, ..., 2.49
lowest_w(ws, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [2.6, 3.9, 5.1, 6.8, 7.6])   # 1.65 (up to rounding)

tests.name: finds the bottom
tests.code:
ws = [0.5 + 0.01 * k for k in range(200)]
out = lowest_w(ws, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [2.6, 3.9, 5.1, 6.8, 7.6])
assert out is not None, 'returned None: did you update best_w inside the loop?'
assert abs(out - 1.65) < 1e-9, f'the bottom of this curve on the grid is w = 1.65, got {out}'

tests.name: exact data
tests.code:
out = lowest_w([1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5], [1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6])
assert out == 2.0, f'y = 2x fits exactly, so w = 2.0 should win; got {out}'

tests.name: smallest, not largest
tests.code:
out = lowest_w([-3.0, 0.0, 3.0], [1, 2], [0.1, 0.2])
assert out == 0.0, f'w = 0 is closest to the data (slope 0.1); got {out}. Keep the candidate with the smallest loss'

hints: if loss < best_loss: best_w, best_loss = w, loss

problems.title: The whole landscape at once (NumPy shapes)
problems.prompt:
Compute the loss on a whole grid of (w, b) settings without loops, using broadcasting with three axes:

  • W[:, None, None] has shape (m, 1, 1)
  • B[None, :, None] has shape (1, k, 1)
  • x[None, None, :] and y[None, None, :] have shape (1, 1, n)

So y - (W*x + B) has shape (m, k, n). Square it and average over the last axis to get the surface of shape (m, k).

Write loss_surface(W, B, x, y) returning that (m, k) array.

W = np.linspace(0.6, 2.0, 141); B = np.linspace(-0.5, 3.5, 401)
L = loss_surface(W, B, np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], float), np.array([2.6, 3.9, 5.1, 6.8, 7.6]))
L.shape                       # (141, 401)
i, j = np.unravel_index(L.argmin(), L.shape)
W[i], B[j]                    # about (1.29, 1.33)

tests.name: matches the formula
tests.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], float); y = np.array([2.6, 3.9, 5.1, 6.8, 7.6])
L = loss_surface(np.array([1.0, 1.5]), np.array([0.0, 0.5]), x, y)
exp = np.mean((y - (1.5 * x + 0.5)) ** 2)
assert abs(L[1, 1] - exp) < 1e-12, f'L[1, 1] should be the loss at w = 1.5, b = 0.5 ({exp:.4f}), got {L[1, 1]}. Check which axis holds W and which holds B'

tests.name: finds the best fit
tests.code:
import numpy as np
W = np.linspace(0.6, 2.0, 141); B = np.linspace(-0.5, 3.5, 401)
L = loss_surface(W, B, np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], float), np.array([2.6, 3.9, 5.1, 6.8, 7.6]))
i, j = np.unravel_index(L.argmin(), L.shape)
assert abs(W[i] - 1.29) < 0.011 and abs(B[j] - 1.33) < 0.011, f'the lowest point should be near (1.29, 1.33), got ({W[i]:.2f}, {B[j]:.2f})'
